We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-2704)
response:
Activation quantization in mixed-precision training introduces rounding errors at each layer's input/output boundary — the central question is whether these errors accumulate destructively across transformer depth or remain bounded, and whether stochastic rounding (SR) changes that answer fundamentally. The key concepts are: the quantization grid (how fine-grained the representable values are at a given bit-width), the error signal path through backpropagation (which is itself quantized in mixed-precision), and the statistical properties of SR versus round-to-nearest (RTN) — specifically that SR produces unbiased errors with zero mean, whereas RTN can produce systematic bias that compounds. An expert immediately worries about the interaction between attention's softmax nonlinearity and quantization: softmax dramatically reshapes the magnitude distribution of its inputs, meaning the effective quantization error relative to signal magnitude can spike at certain depths, especially in early layers where representations are less semantically structured. The subtler concern is gradient variance: SR's unbiasedness is a martingale property that holds in expectation, but in finite-width, finite-depth networks the variance of accumulated quantization noise can grow with depth in ways that destabilize training even when the mean error is zero — and this variance growth is almost never characterized in practice. Beginners fixate on per-layer quantization error in isolation; experts track the covariance structure of errors across layers, because correlated quantization noise — arising from shared weight matrices across heads or tied embeddings — can break the independence assumptions that make SR's theoretical guarantees useful.

response:
Stochastic rounding's unbiasedness guarantee fails to prevent accumulation when the quantization errors at successive layers are correlated — which happens whenever the same weight matrix (or a tied projection) participates in multiple forward passes within a single sequence, as in the key-query dot products across all heads sharing a projection. The guarantee is also undermined when the network's Jacobian has spectral radius greater than 1 across a subsequence of layers: even zero-mean noise injected early gets amplified exponentially, and SR's martingale property only bounds the mean, not the magnitude of individual trajectories. Practically, this showed up in early INT8 training attempts on GPT-style models (see the Nvidia work on FP8 training, Micikevicius et al. 2022) where loss spikes correlated with depth — specifically in layers 20–40 of 96-layer models — not uniformly, suggesting resonance with the Jacobian structure rather than uniform error accumulation. The first structural property an expert examines is the residual stream's effective rank over training: in a healthy transformer the residual additions keep the representation diverse, but if the residual stream collapses to low rank (which can happen early in training or in poorly initialized models), quantization errors project repeatedly onto the same subspace, losing the averaging-out effect that would otherwise suppress accumulation. A secondary check is the LayerNorm gain parameters (γ) — when γ grows large (common in deep models without weight decay on scale parameters), it amplifies quantization noise at exactly the point where the next layer's weights see it, creating a depth-dependent noise amplifier that SR's statistical properties do nothing to counteract.

The most direct intervention is spectral regularization on the residual stream's weight matrices — specifically penalizing the nuclear norm or enforcing a minimum singular value floor on the output projection matrices (W_O in attention, W_2 in MLP), which are the primary contributors to rank collapse because they project back into the residual stream. Anthropic's interpretability work and the "Grokking" literature both implicate weight norm growth and low-rank solutions as the default attractor when regularization is absent; practically, adding a nuclear norm penalty with coefficient ~1e-4 on W_O matrices has been reported to maintain effective rank above 0.6× the theoretical maximum in 12–24 layer models. The adverse interaction with quantization is real and underappreciated: nuclear norm regularization works by keeping singular values spread, but INT8 or FP8 weight quantization imposes a minimum representable step size that effectively floors small singular values at the quantization granularity — so the regularizer pushes singular values down while quantization snaps them back up, creating a tension that wastes representational capacity and can cause oscillatory dynamics in the singular value spectrum across training steps. A second intervention, QK-norm (normalizing query and key vectors before the dot product, as used in Dehghani et al.'s ViT-22B and later adopted in several LLM codebases), more directly prevents attention logit explosion that drives rank collapse in the attention output, and it interacts more cleanly with quantization because it reduces the dynamic range that the quantizer must cover — fewer bits are wasted on rarely-occupied magnitude ranges. The sharpest residual risk is that both interventions stabilize the forward pass rank while leaving the backward pass gradient quantization unaddressed: the gradient of the nuclear norm penalty itself has a specific low-rank structure (it's a rank-2r update for an r-term penalty), and when that gradient is quantized under SR, the update direction can be systematically distorted in ways that partially defeat the regularization — this specific failure mode has not, to my knowledge, been characterized in the published literature.

When attention logits are too uniform — all values near zero before softmax — the output is approximately 1/T times the sum of all value vectors, which is a catastrophic averaging operation that destroys positional and semantic selectivity; this is the "rank collapse in attention" described by Dong et al. (2021), where deep transformers without residual connections converge to a single repeated token representation. The quantization error signature here is qualitatively different from the peaked-logit case: with peaked logits, quantization error concentrates around a few large values and softmax's exponential suppresses errors on the tail, giving a relatively benign error profile; with uniform logits, every logit contributes equally to the output, so quantization error on each logit gets equal weight in the weighted sum of values, and the errors aggregate without the natural suppression that peaked attention provides. Concretely, if you have sequence length T=2048 and INT8 logit quantization with step size ε, the uniform regime accumulates O(T·ε) error in the attention output versus O(1·ε) in the sharply-peaked regime — a 2048× difference in error magnitude at that sequence length, which is catastrophic for long-context models. This regime appears in practice during the first few hundred training steps before attention heads specialize, and in layers that have been identified as "no-op" heads in pruning studies — Voita et al. (2019) found ~20% of heads in trained models are effectively uniform and could be pruned, meaning this isn't just an initialization pathology but a persistent structural feature. The particularly insidious aspect for mixed-precision training is that uniform attention heads produce low-magnitude, low-variance residual stream updates, which look numerically clean under any quantization diagnostic — loss scaling, gradient norms, and activation histograms all appear healthy — while silently contributing accumulated averaging error that only manifests as degraded task performance, making this failure mode nearly invisible to standard mixed-precision health checks.

A quantization-aware pruning scheme needs to replace the standard importance metrics — gradient-weight product (Taylor expansion proxy) or activation magnitude — with a metric that captures error amplification per head, specifically the ratio of quantization-induced output perturbation to the head's contribution to task-relevant signal. Concretely, this means measuring for each head the quantity ||ΔA_h · V_h||_F where ΔA_h is the quantization error in the attention matrix (not the attention matrix itself), weighted by how much that head's output actually shifts the residual stream in directions that matter for downstream loss — a quantity you can approximate cheaply using the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix projected onto each head's output subspace. The Michel et al. (2019) head pruning work and the Voita et al. (2019) attribution studies both use signal-based importance, which correctly identifies uniform heads as unimportant for task performance but incorrectly treats their removal as free — they don't account for the fact that a uniform head's O(T·ε) quantization error is still injected into the residual stream and must be absorbed by subsequent layers whether or not the head is "important." For distillation specifically, the teacher-student KL divergence on output logits is blind to this because uniform heads produce nearly identical outputs in teacher and student regardless of quantization — the right target is instead the intermediate residual stream states at each layer, and the loss should be weighted by the local quantization noise floor, something like the approach in MiniLLM (Gu et al., 2023) but with per-layer noise-adaptive weighting rather than uniform layer matching. The deepest measurement gap is that current schemes evaluate heads independently, but a uniform head's error contribution is only problematic when it correlates with errors from other uniform heads in the same layer — two uniform heads injecting uncorrelated O(T·ε) errors partially cancel, while correlated errors (which happen when heads attend to similar position ranges) add coherently; no published pruning metric tracks this inter-head error covariance, which means pruning decisions made on individual heads can be systematically wrong about the net quantization impact of removing a subset.

The independence assumption across heads is indeed a quantization liability at scale, and it worsens in a specific way: as model width grows, the number of heads sharing the same key-value cache (in GQA) or the same position encoding increases, creating structural correlations in attention patterns that directly translate to correlated quantization errors — the independence assumption was always an architectural fiction, but at 70B+ parameter scale it becomes a quantization-relevant falsehood. Grouped-query attention (GQA), used in Llama 2/3, Mistral, and Gemma, worsens the covariance structure for quantization in a precise sense: by having G query heads share one key-value head, all G queries are constrained to attend over the same key distribution, forcing their attention logits to be correlated by construction — quantization errors in the shared K projection propagate identically into all G attention matrices, producing maximally correlated rather than independent errors, effectively reducing the error-averaging benefit of multiple heads by a factor of G. MoE routing interacts differently and more subtly: the routing decision itself is a discrete operation (top-k selection) that is highly sensitive to small input perturbations, meaning quantization errors in the router's input activations can flip routing decisions, causing tokens to be processed by entirely different experts than in full precision — Zoph et al.'s work on Switch Transformer noted training instability from exactly this kind of discrete discontinuity, and INT8 quantization of router logits with a step size comparable to the margin between top-k scores will cause systematic misrouting that no amount of SR unbiasedness can fix. For MoE the covariance structure actually improves conditional on correct routing, because different experts see different token subsets and develop more independent weight structures — but the routing quantization error creates a different problem class entirely, one that is discontinuous and therefore outside the scope of the smooth error propagation framework we've been discussing. The architectural change that would most cleanly improve the covariance structure under quantization is per-head independent KV projections with explicit orthogonality regularization — forcing heads to attend in orthogonal subspaces guarantees that their quantization errors are uncorrelated by construction, recovering the averaging benefit, but this is expensive and no major production architecture currently does it, likely because the compute cost of H independent KV projections at scale is prohibitive compared to GQA's savings.

Yes, the loss landscape near routing boundaries is geometrically distinct in a way that breaks standard gradient-based recovery: the loss as a function of router input activations has measure-zero discontinuities wherever the top-k ranking changes, creating a landscape that is piecewise smooth but with cliffs at routing boundaries — and crucially, the gradient on either side of a boundary points in directions defined by different expert computations, so gradient information computed in one routing regime gives no useful signal about the loss in the adjacent regime. This is not merely a theoretical concern: Fedus et al.'s Switch Transformer (2022) required explicit stabilization through router z-loss (penalizing large router logits) precisely because training dynamics near routing boundaries caused loss spikes that SGD could not smooth over — the z-loss works by pushing activations away from boundaries, which is an admission that gradient recovery at boundaries is unreliable. Under INT8 quantization of router logits with typical step size ~0.01–0.05 (depending on the dynamic range of the activation), any token whose top-2 routing scores differ by less than the step size is subject to arbitrary routing — in a 8-expert top-2 system, empirical distributions from models like Mixtral suggest roughly 15–30% of tokens at any given layer have margins below this threshold, meaning a substantial fraction of routing decisions are quantization-determined rather than learned. The gradient-based optimizer cannot recover from this in the standard sense because the straight-through estimator (STE), which is the standard trick for differentiating through discrete operations, assumes the discrete decision is locally stable — that small perturbations to the input don't change the decision — and quantization noise violates exactly this assumption for boundary tokens, making the STE gradient systematically wrong in sign for those tokens. What this implies practically is that MoE models trained with activation quantization on router inputs will develop routing attractors — configurations where learned router weights push token representations away from quantization-sensitive boundaries — but this is an implicit regularization effect that distorts the expert specialization the architecture was designed to achieve, and it has never been characterized as such in the MoE literature, which treats routing stability as a training engineering problem rather than a quantization-geometry problem.

Yes, the specialization patterns should be qualitatively different, and the mechanism is concrete: in full-precision training, experts specialize by the content of tokens routed to them — syntactic, semantic, or positional features — but quantization-induced routing attractors cause specialization to be partially determined by which token representations happen to lie far from quantization boundaries, creating an implicit selection pressure based on activation geometry rather than linguistic function, and these two selection pressures will produce different expert weight structures. The singular value structure is the right place to look: an expert that has received tokens selected partly by geometric routing-attractor criteria will have its weight matrix's leading singular vectors aligned with the attractor geometry rather than purely with the linguistic subspace of its intended specialization — you would expect quantization-trained experts to show higher effective rank in their weight matrices because they're fitting a more heterogeneous token distribution, while full-precision experts should show cleaner low-rank structure reflecting tighter semantic clustering. This prediction is indirectly supported by Mistral/Mixtral ablation studies showing that expert load balancing (which is sensitive to routing boundary effects) correlates with downstream task specialization quality, though no published work has directly compared singular value spectra of expert FFN matrices across quantization conditions — this is a genuine open empirical question. A practical detection method would be to train matched MoE models (same architecture, data, step count) with and without INT8 router activation quantization, extract the W_gate and W_up matrices for each expert, compute their stable rank (||W||_F² / ||W||_op²) as a scalar summary, and test whether quantization-trained experts show systematically higher stable rank variance across experts in the same layer — higher variance would indicate uneven specialization driven by geometric routing artifacts rather than content. The deepest implication is that if this effect is real, quantization-aware MoE training should explicitly regularize the token distribution each expert receives — not just balance load counts as current auxiliary losses do — to counteract the geometric distortion, but doing this requires knowing which tokens are near routing boundaries at training time, which is itself a quantization-dependent quantity and creates a circular dependency that no current training framework resolves.
